title.zh: 馬萊塞遠航阿基利內克

region.en: Akilinek, the fabulous country beyond the seas

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; collated from two copies (one East Greenland verbal narration), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 17 'Malaise — The Man who travelled to Akilinek', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Drifted east on the breaking ice with gull amulets, two sisters land on the rich other-country of Akilinek, marry two kayakers who race ashore for them, and escape home over the ice with their babies when one husband threatens death for a daughter — leaving the infants frozen on the snow. Jeered at home for telling nothing, they finally boast of the hunting 'in Akilinek,' and Malaise rows out to it under a threefold-covered boat, laughing his timid wife's tears down. Meeting their escaped husbands, he fills a drinking-tub with water dusted with hairs from dead men's reindeer-skin stockings — each suitor who drinks turns into a reindeer and is shot into the sea, one 'miserable specimen' spared to live on.
summary.zh: 兩姊妹隨碎裂的浮冰東漂，憑海鷗護身符登陸豐饒的阿基利內克，嫁給爭先上岸的兩名皮艇客；因丈夫揚言『再生女兒便殺你』，她們攜嬰越冰而逃，嬰兒凍斃雪中。歸家後，她們起初守口如瓶，飽受譏誚，終於誇口『阿基利內克才是獵人的天堂』。馬萊塞遂以三層皮的艘船西航尋地，途中以亡者馴鹿皮襪之毛混水設壺於敵必經之石——每名前夫喝水即化馴鹿，被他射落海中，獨留一個『可憐的標本』活命傳種。

sensitivity.note: Akilinek is the fabulous country beyond the seas in Greenlandic tradition. Infant deaths and sorcerous killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Malaise was a jolly, fearless fellow who lived in prosperity with his two sisters, both younger than himself, wintering at the mouth of a fiord; when he went out kayaking, his sisters followed him on foot along the beach, returning as soon as they saw him put back. One day, the sea all covered with ice, the sisters went to the outermost islets to gather roots; suddenly an eastern gale overtook them, the ice broke up, and they were taken far out to sea in very bad weather. When the sky cleared they came in sight of high land, drifted to it, and landed safely, almost starving — the ice-floe they had floated on turned to foam behind them. Each had part of a gull for an amulet. Wandering across the country, they came to a little bay into which a river emptied: 'There will be salmon yonder, I warrant, or there would not be so many gulls about.' The river abounded in salmon; catching one they made a fire by rubbing wood, fried the fish on a slab, and were quite satisfied with half the tail-piece. At low tide the beach turned quite dry, covered with spotted seals and various other kinds, of which they killed as many as they required with big stones, and took up their abode there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 17 'Malaise'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day two kayakers hunting spotted seals, seeing the girls, were heard to exclaim, 'Well, he who gets ashore first shall marry the prettiest of the two'; both took to their paddles, he who first reached the shore touching the elder sister, the other taking the younger — and quite forgetting their hunt, they hastened home to fetch a boat, returning with a good crew and bringing the girls to their house, where they lived as happy as could be for some time. After a while each had a daughter; but the eldest noticed her sister had quite lost her spirits, and asked why she was always sobbing and crying: her husband had told her he would kill her if she next time bore him a daughter. 'We'll pack up our clothes, and as soon as the ice forms, we'll return to our old home; but don't let them suspect anything.' They made themselves new clothes and put them by in bags concealed beneath the boat outside; the seal-hunting ceased, the men went out visiting and dancing at a large house close by, and the sisters waited a convenient opportunity. One dance-night, when nobody was to be seen outside, they walked up and down lulling their children to sleep in short breeches only; the little girls who used to nurse the children ran out after them, but were drawn in by a funny song — and the sisters hastened to the boat, put the babies into their amowts, and started.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 17 'Malaise'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Keeping on shore at first, then out on the ice, they wandered all night long, hiding behind blocks of ice at daybreak when they heard the sound of sledges following their traces. Where their footprints were lost, their pursuers halted and called out, 'Your poor little children are crying for you'; they did not leave their retreat until evening, then set forth and continued their journey — but on the way they suffered their babies to freeze to death, and having put them down on the snow, left them there. Reaching land, they recognised the place of their former winter-station, and behold, their own little house just as they had left it. Malaise was very much astonished to see his sisters entering, and questioned them about Akilinek and the hunting in those parts, but he could not make them tell anything. After their return he displayed great energy in fishing and hunting, until the days began to lengthen, when the sisters turned to him: 'Though almost nothing is to be got in this poor country, it cannot be denied that Malaise strives hard enough to provide for us; but, to be sure, in Akilinek there is something for a hunter.' Then they told him all he wished; even in fine weather Malaise did not stir out, and when they had told him of the many seals found on the dry beach he could not forbear: 'I really must try Akilinek — in spring when the saddleback-seals appear. I will give my women's boat a threefold covering.' His wife began crying, being of a very timid disposition; but Malaise only laughed at her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 17 'Malaise'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as the saddleback-seals appeared he caught as many as they wanted for boat-covers, got the three coverings, and waited a favourable opportunity. One windless morning: 'The day is fine and it is quite calm now; let us be off for Akilinek' — his wife again crying, laughed down. Pushing off westward, the sisters rowed all by themselves while their sister-in-law cried in the bottom of the boat; to tease her further Malaise rose and looked aft, observing, 'I think we are going to have a gale, it is getting quite black out there!' — and she cried in good earnest, to his very great diversion. Having lost sight of their own country, he found they went too slow and cut the outer covering away because it had grown too wet; before sighting any land he likewise cut off the second cover, then suddenly sprang to his feet: 'I see the loom of the land yonder!' His wife got up and stuck to the oars bravely. Coming close to the land, the sisters recognised the bay where they had first landed, and observed their former husbands coming on to attack them. Before their departure Malaise had been out to the grave of some relative in search of a pair of reindeer-skin stockings, brought away with him; he now took a drinking-vessel, filled it with water, poured in some dust mingled with the hairs of the stockings, and put the tub down on an adjacent rock their adversaries were obliged to pass. When the eldest came up he took a drink — and was at once transformed into a reindeer, shot by Malaise and rolled into the sea; the other had no better luck. In this manner Malaise killed all their companions excepting one, to whom he said, 'I will spare thee that thou mayst live on, a miserable specimen of thy countrymen.' Some time afterwards he again gave his boat three separate coverings, filled it with narwhal-horns, matak, salmon, and many other valuables, and reached his former home, where he stayed content until his death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 17 'Malaise'; not verbatim.

title.en: Navaranak or Javraganak: The Go-Between Who Made Enemies Friends
title.zh: 納瓦拉納克：挑撥兩族的通譯女

region.en: Interior and coast boundary, North Greenland / Okak, Labrador
region.zh: 北格陵蘭內陸與海岸交界／拉布拉多奧卡克島

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; two separate narratives (North Greenland; Labrador, Okak island), English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 18 'Navaranak or Javraganak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The servant-maid Navaranak, tired of ferrying matak and tallow between inlanders and coast-people, tells each side the other is preparing invasion — until the inlanders fall on the coast villages while the men are out hunting, mothers killing their own children in fright, a pregnant woman bribing her way free beneath the ledge. Dragged to death behind a rope when she is caught, Navaranak's murder is avenged on her whole people in a lake-surrounded arrow-battle. In the Labrador variant the Indian servant Javraganak brings her 'many brothers' on a night the murmuring outside is mistaken for hares on the house-tops, and she is dragged to death by an angakok-made road through a mountain.
summary.zh: 通譯女納瓦拉納克厭倦了在內陸人與海濱人之間往返運送鯨皮與鹿脂，便向雙方謊稱對方將入侵——內陸人終於趁男獵女守之際血洗海濱村落，母親們惶恐中親手殺死自己的孩子；一名孕婦以全部家產換得免死。她被繩索拖拽至死，族人隨即遠征湖畔內陸營地，箭戰全殲其族。拉布拉多流本中，印第安僕女雅夫拉加納克於野兔奔騰之夜引來族人屠村，最後亦被拖曳致死。

sensitivity.note: Rink's variants localize the same events: North Greenland inlanders, Labrador Indians, and a South Greenland version identifying the inlanders with the ancient Scandinavian settlers. Graphic massacre recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: The inlanders and the coast-people in the beginning were friends. A servant-maid called Navaranak used to be sent out by the inlanders to the coast-people to fetch back matak (edible whale-skin), and in exchange brought them reindeer-tallow; but after a time she grew weary of this work, and resolved to free herself by making them enemies. For this purpose she told the inlanders that the coast-people were going to attack them, and to the coasters she asserted that the inlanders were making ready to invade them. At length she provoked the inlanders to such a degree that they resolved upon attacking the coast-people, choosing a time when they were well aware the men had all gone out hunting; accompanied by Navaranak, they fell upon the helpless women and children. In their fright some of the mothers killed their own children, but one woman who was pregnant fled down beneath the ledge; and when Navaranak was sent back by the inlanders to find her out, she promised her all she possessed not to betray her. Some also escaped by hiding among the rocks, but all the rest were killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 18 'Navaranak or Javraganak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the men returned, those left alive ran down and told them what had happened; coming up from the beach and beholding all their dead, the men were almost desperate. When the time came for flensing and cutting up the whale, Navaranak did not arrive as usual — she seemed to have disappeared altogether. When summer had come round, the men prepared a great many arrows and set out for the interior to take revenge on the inlanders. On their way they called out, as was their wont, 'Navaranak, come on; we have got matak for thee!' but no one appeared; again they went on a good distance, then repeatedly called out — and this time she answered the summons and went up to them. Noticing their arrows, she was about to take flight; reassuring her, they told her she had no need to do that. When she had ventured quite close, they asked where her countrymen were to be found — 'Further away in the interior of the country!' — but now they made her fast to a rope and dragged her along with them until she perished. They arrived at a very large lake where the tents of the inlanders were pitched all around, waited till all had entered the tents, and made their attack: arrows came flying from both sides, but those of the inlanders soon grew fewer, and the coast-people remained all unwounded. When they had done with the men they went inside, killing women and children; and having thus satisfied their revenge, returned to their homes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 18 'Navaranak or Javraganak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the island of Okak, in Labrador, this tale is told as follows: At Kivalek, on the island of Okak, there once lived a great many people, among whom was an Indian woman named Javraganak. From her childhood she had lived with the coast-people as their servant, but had always remained a stranger among them. One day when she was hungry and longed for one of her Indian dishes, she said, 'At Pangma my countrymen have plenty of tongues' — an old man sneeringly replied, 'I daresay thou hast many brothers and relatives away there; thou hadst better make them come over here,' and at night she wandered away to give them warning. In those times hares were very abundant, and sometimes you might even hear them run about on the house-tops. One night Javraganak came with a great number of her countrymen; those within heard a murmuring sound outside, and the old man said, 'Well, if that is not the hares again! They are very lively, it seems.' Besides him there was not a man at home, all being out hunting — and so it happened that all the inhabitants were put to death by Javraganak's Indian countrymen, many seeking refuge in a cave, where some were suffocated and others murdered. On their return the men found their wives and children all killed, but shortly afterwards set out to kill the murderers. Among these men was an angakok who made a road for them right through a mountain, and the countrymen of Javraganak were all destroyed. She, however, was not to be found, having gone to hide herself; but the men had great trust in their angakok. At last a man happened to call out, 'How I wish that Javraganak would serve me again!' — upon which she immediately appeared, looking very comfortable. They all fell upon her, wound a cord around her body, and dragged her along the ground till she died; and in this way she was paid back for what she had done to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 18 'Navaranak or Javraganak'; not verbatim.

title.en: Avarunguak or Agdlerut: Wintering Among Bears in Human Shape
title.zh: 阿瓦龍瓦克：與人形之熊同冬

region.en: Southern auk-coast and the country behind the mountains
region.zh: 南方海鳩海岸與群山彼端

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Court-hunted from his pinching village, Avarunguak steers for the forbidden huge tent and winter with a family of five-windowed giants who eat his walruses, feed him from their own stores, and exam every whelp's joints — the seventh alone 'perfect.' He proves himself by licking out all the lamp-oil, joins their raid on their enemies, slips away at the prescribed moment, and sees his hosts turn to bears pursuing — until his salmon amulet makes him too slippery to catch. Leaving in spring, he learns the truth: they had been wintering among bears in human shape, and the people who later killed a bear sealed the family's doom.
summary.zh: 因村中捏人取樂之風被眾人追逐的阿瓦龍瓦克，反而駕舟投宿被禁的五窗巨宅，與五口之家過冬——巨人家族吃掉他的海象、以自家存糧養他，逐只檢視狗崽關節，唯第七只『四肢俱全』。他以舔盡全屋燈油證明自己，隨其出征仇敵；在指定時刻藉口出屋逃走，回頭只見主人一家化熊緊追——幸而他以鮭魚為護身符，滑溜難捉。翌春辭別時，他們囑咐：『無論去哪裡，告訴人們見熊不可殺。』——原來這一家人本就是人形之熊；南方殺熊的消息傳來，他們的命運便已註定。

sensitivity.note: Bears-in-human-shape motif (compare Rink tale 6/30 note on the great bear). The bear-taboo injunction is a core Greenlandic hunting ethic.

passages.text: At a well-peopled place the trick of pinching was a favourite amusement with the inhabitants. One night a girl, an only sister with a number of brothers, came running in crying, 'I wonder who it can possibly be who is always running after me and paying court to me?' — they told her to bring him into the house next time. When she brought him in, it was a man totally unknown to all of them: Avarunguak had grown up in solitary places, and when he came among people he married this girl, learned to manage a kayak, and grew an excellent hunter. Once they had visitors from the south, and an old woman of the party accosted him: 'If Avarunguak were to hear of the nice hunt, and the many auks we have down in the south, I am sure he would be wanting to go there!' He could not sleep for the desire to go at once, and the next morning ordered his housemates to make ready for the voyage south.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way out, the people they encountered all made answer that the place was not very nigh yet; at a resting-place they were told: 'When ye leave here, and have doubled the cape, ye will come in sight of a very large tent — this ye must shun; but soon afterwards ye will perceive a little white point, and having also passed this, ye will fall in with a great many people. To those ye shall go up.' Avarunguak steered his boat towards the large tent, unheeding the advice of his companions; a huge man came out receiving them very civilly: 'It is really a matter of difficulty to get any one to keep company with here; pray stay and live with me' — and they prepared for wintering there. Every morning Avarunguak awoke early, but somehow his housemate was always out and off before him; when the auks came screaming across the country the huge man bade him shut the curtain closely so only one bird could get in at a time, and not begin to catch any of them until the tent was quite full. Avarunguak began catching them too soon, the birds instantly left, and he heard the man scolding — 'Didst thou not mind my telling thee that thou wert not to catch them till the tent was quite full, lest I should be in want of food?' — still, he had got a great many birds, quite sufficient to live upon for a good length of time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the walrus time came, the big man warned he did not pursue them — 'the red walrus is a very ferocious beast, and at that time I do not venture out at all' — but Avarunguak grew very excited and lanced his first walrus; his big companion came down to the beach, took half of the walrus, dragged it along with only one hand past Avarunguak's tent, and carried it off to his own, where he sat eating it all by himself while his wife and daughter only looked on. Next time the big man's wife carried off his prize, and after her their three daughters did the same by turns; not until they had all got their walrus did they desist. In the beginning of winter Avarunguak always caught plenty, but the big man, having no kayak of his own, never went out; the sea froze up and all hunting ceased. 'Here we are all badly off; but I know that behind our country there is good hunting enough, and thither we intend to go to-morrow.' Asked how swift he might be — 'I think I can run a race with any of the quadrupeds' — he was taken along only after much beseeching, all carrying cords of sealskin round their necks. Crossing the mountains they beheld a bare land, and the big man spoke: 'Dost thou see yonder lofty mountains far away? Behind, there is a sea where the white whale in abundance are found; but when we get so far, thou must only aim at the small ones, because thou wilt not be expert enough to carry home one of the larger ones.' The daughters had to take hold of Avarunguak by his arms to help him along; at the appointed place each watched at a cleft in the ice — no sooner did Avarunguak see a huge white whale rise than he aimed at and killed it, while the others each brought up two fish. Scolded for disobeying, he was to have his fish tied to theirs and be dragged home sitting on top of it — 'Since I commenced hunting I have never let my game be carried home by any one but myself, nor shall I do so now. I have caught the fish myself, and will take care to bring it home' — and they let him have his own way, disappearing from his sight as if blown away. It was evening and again beginning to dawn before he could see his home, meeting the others coming back to fish anew; not till the fourth day did he get home, having been obliged to eat all the matak of his dolphin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: About this time Avarunguak's people had a dog that happened to whelp. When the first whelp appeared, the huge man whispered something to his wife, on which she brought it him, and he took hold of it and examined all its joints; each new-born whelp was brought to him to be examined in the same way, but when they had handled the seventh — the last — they were heard saying, 'This one is perfect; there is not a limb wanting.' From that time they seemed despondent; Avarunguak, beginning to fear their intentions, one day said to them, 'If you would like to have a dog, you are welcome to take the one you like best' — they chose the last born and became so fond of it that they let it stop on the ledge and sleep beside them at night, and from this time Avarunguak himself became a great favourite. While the winter lasted the big man spoke as follows: 'We intend soon to go and visit our enemies.' Avarunguak was very desirous to join, but was told, 'No, friend; thou wouldst too soon be worn out: for, in the first place, thou canst not eat blubber and flesh enough; and secondly, because of thy clumsiness and want of speed' — 'As to the blubber and flesh, methinks I do well enough as regards both of them' — 'Well, then, try to lick out the oil of all the lamps here, beginning with the outermost.' Avarunguak succeeded, and a few days after was told he might accompany them. The instructions: when they have entered and begin licking the oil, he must help; they will each be presented with one large white fish, and he must thrust his knife into it, turn it round, put the cut piece into his mouth, and suddenly exclaim, 'I must go outside, but I will be back in a moment, and go on eating; I enjoy it very much' — but when outside take to his heels and run for home as fast as possible, and before he has been off long, they shall empty the lamps and soon overtake him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some time after, they carried out their intention of visiting their enemies in their place of abode, setting about licking the oil of the lamps, Avarunguak joining them to the best of his ability. When the hosts saw a stranger among their visitors they regarded him keenly, so the huge man interposed, 'That is a new housemate of ours; he is living with us at present, and assists us every way' — praising and flattering him very much, making a great deal of his dexterity and strength, adding he was more than a match for them every way, anything but the truth, but they dared not do otherwise for fear of their enemies. 'Bring in the meal for the visitors' — large white fish were brought in, the guests soon fell to; but Avarunguak forgot he had been advised to leave off in good time, never remembering till he was quite satisfied, then quickly pronouncing the words he had been told, took himself off and commenced running as fast as possible. Coming near their own house he turned round and saw that the creatures he had been visiting were transformed into bears, pursuing him closely; his own housemates soon overtook him, the daughters again taking him by the arms to speed him on. When they had almost reached the house the enemies seemed at their very heels, and Avarunguak was deserted by his protectors, who gave him a blow so that he fell, and the bears instantly gathered round him — but he chanced to have a salmon for his amulet, and this did him good service in making him too slippery to be caught hold of, and thus he escaped. When spring came round, Avarunguak took a fancy to remove to another place; on departing, his huge companion said to him, 'I hope thou wilt soon return and stay with us; but wherever thou goest, mind to tell the people never to kill a bear when one appears.' Thus they departed — but on turning round they now saw that their housemates too had been transformed into bears: they had been wintering among bears in human shape. Later on they heard that some people in the south had killed a bear, and still later Avarunguak and his wife died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 19 'Avarunguak or Agdlerut'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Girl Who Married an Atliarusek

region.en: Outermost islet and rock-dwelling of the atliarusek, Greenland fiord
region.zh: 格陵蘭峽灣最外島與岩中人居所

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 20 'The Girl who married an Atliarusek', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Scorned by the suitors who nearly killed him for refusing to give up his daughter, a selfish old man winters on an outermost islet — where his daughter is secretly wed to an atliarusek, an elf of the sea-shore rocks, who keeps out of sight, then brings home hunting-lines and beach-loads of seals. Joining his people, the couple's boats dive beneath the waves past the inhabited places, load up with reindeer; and when the old man fetches his former mockers to a feast, he quotes their own taunts back to them: 'Your words were these: Thou wilt surely never get a clever husband for thy daughter. But you see I have, for all that. Now help yourself, if ye please, and eat as much as ever ye like.'
summary.zh: 因不肯交出女兒而被求婚者毒打的老人遭全村嘲笑，攜家遷居最外小島過冬——女兒卻已秘密嫁給岩中人阿特利亞烏塞克。他先是隱形，繼而懸起獵繩、沙灘上滿是海豹；春日同行，舟隊竟能潛入波下穿過有人居住之地，滿載馴鹿而歸。老人隨後將昔日嘲笑他的人全數接來設宴，把當年的話擲回他們面前：『你們說：你這女兒休想嫁個好獵手。可你看，我偏偏找到了。現在請隨意吃喝吧。』

sensitivity.note: Atliarusek (probably = ingnersuak) are elves or gnomes with abodes in rocks along the sea-shore, per Rink's note. Boat-diving motif parallels the inland-dweller corpus.

passages.text: An aged couple had a daughter who had a great many suitors; but the old people were very selfish and wanted to keep her at home. Meanwhile a man came who was very anxious to get the daughter; at last he fought them, and had nearly killed them — the old man escaped into his boat. The other men of the place despised and scorned him, but he got the boat loaded and left, the others shouting contemptuously, 'It won't be easy for thee to get a husband for thy daughter! The poor old thing, who is quite unable to hunt — he to dare reject any one! Only let him come to be in want of necessaries, and then look out if there be any one to help him!' He set off without deigning to answer, and landed at one of the outermost islets, where they built their house and put up for the winter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 20 'The Girl who married an Atliarusek'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One morning the old man awoke saying, 'I wonder what I have just been seeing? Methinks I saw a man gliding through the doorway'; he questioned his daughter, but she kept silence, and he got suspicious. Next morning he saw a real man slip out of the doorway, and on being closely questioned the daughter confessed that she was married to an atliarusek — 'For fear thou wouldst not like him, he keeps out of sight; but if thou dost not mind, he will come and live with us.' The father said it was all right, and he might come at once; towards evening the daughter several times left the room, returning at last with a hunting-line hung up on a nail to dry — he had returned and brought home the produce of his hunt, but must take some part of it to his relatives. Outside they saw many seals on the beach, and rejoiced very much at their sudden prosperity. The following morning the old man beheld the stranger reposing beside his daughter; the son-in-law had already taken himself off whenever the old man stirred. 'Why do you not make him come and stay with us? We like him very well indeed' — and in the evening when he again returned with his catch, he went inside and made himself at home, the parents very civil to him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 20 'The Girl who married an Atliarusek'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In spring he wanted to go further inland along the fiord-side, as was generally his custom, but told them he was obliged to join his parents, being their only son, and as such ought not to let his sisters be without protection. When they again met, he told them they were now ready for starting; the father-in-law likewise put his boat into the water, and as they were going to set off, another boat appeared coming straight out of the beach — both went along together and made the land at the same time in the evening. Next morning they started again; approaching an inhabited place, the head-man of the atliaruseks told them always to keep close in their wake, and all of a sudden they saw his boat sink beneath the surface and totally disappear. The old man got rather frightened; but on arriving at the spot their boat dived down in the same manner, without any damage to the crew, catching sight of their companions' boat right ahead — they continued their course beneath the waves of the sea. Having safely passed the inhabited places, they once more rose to the surface and continued their voyage without further peril; arriving at their place of destination, they went reindeer-hunting and got their boats fully laden. Wintering again, the son-in-law provided amply for them, and they prospered and were well off.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 20 'The Girl who married an Atliarusek'; not verbatim.

passages.text: About this time intelligence reached them that the men who had once scorned and abused them were living in great want, and the old man determined to help them: he loaded his kayak with matak and brought it to them. They asked whence he had got it — whether it was not taken from the carcass of a whale driven on shore accidentally; he left without deigning an answer, and talking the matter over at home the son-in-law exclaimed, 'I should really like to have a look at these people' — so the old man went back to fetch all the men who had formerly been his daughter's suitors, returning with a large train of kayaks following him. They landed and were very hospitably received and regaled with reindeer-meat and seal-flesh; when they had satisfied their appetite, the old man accosted them: 'I wonder if ye can still remember what ye were telling me a long time ago when ye had nearly killed me, wanting by main force my daughter for your wife? Your words were these: Thou wilt surely never get a clever husband for thy daughter. But you see I have, for all that. Likewise ye said that ye would deny me your assistance if ever I came in want: now help yourself, if ye please, and eat as much as ever ye like.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 20 'The Girl who married an Atliarusek'; not verbatim.
